_about: Every number used by person.py and reach.py. Each block says where it comes from. 'assumption' means no source was found yet: these are the first values to calibrate against solved cases.

terrain._source: Wood, Mackaness, Simpson, Armstrong (2023), Improved prediction of hiking speeds using a data driven approach, Table 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16065. Speed km/h = exp(a + b*theta + c*theta^2 + d*phi); theta = walking slope in the direction of travel (deg, uphill positive), phi = hill slope of the terrain (deg). Fitted on 88,000 km of UK walking GPS tracks (average walker, breaks removed).
terrain._flat_reference: exp(1.580): the model's speed on flat paved ground; a person's own flat speed is divided by this to scale the whole model.

landcover._source: ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200 classes, https://esa-worldcover.org/en/data-access (CC BY 4.0). Class -> Wood terrain class. 'extra' multiplies speed on top of the Wood class and is an ASSUMPTION: the Wood data only contains walkable ground, so it has no case for pushing through dense maquis, closed forest or marsh.

osm_ways._source: OpenStreetMap highway=* (ODbL). surface=* overrides the default when present. A way is burned into every grid cell it crosses, after water, so bridges stay passable.

walk_speed_adult._source: Bohannon & Andrews (2011), Normal walking speed: a descriptive meta-analysis, Physiotherapy 97:182-189, doi:10.1016/j.physio.2010.12.004; values by decade as reproduced in the University of Toronto iWalk guide. Comfortable gait on a walkway, m/s.

walk_speed_child._source: Ages 2-4: Pediatric Physical Therapy 2015 normative table (0.93 / 0.99 / 1.14 m/s for 24-35, 36-47, 48-59 months), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4580974/table/T2. Ages 7-11: 1.05 and 1.11 m/s quoted in Genij Ortopedii (Ilizarov journal) from older references (single source). Ages 13-19 interpolated to the adult value (assumption).

modifiers._source: ASSUMPTION unless stated. speed multiplies flat walking speed; sens multiplies the slope and hill-slope terms of the terrain model (1 = the average walker of Wood 2023, 1.5 = slopes cost half again as much); max_climb is the steepest walking slope (deg) the person can go up or down at all.
modifiers._hill_over_climb: ASSUMPTION. Off paths, a cell whose hill slope exceeds max_climb + this many degrees is impassable even when traversed at an angle (zig-zagging lowers the walking slope, not the steepness of the ground underfoot).

running._source: ASSUMPTION. Flat running speed (km/h) and how many minutes in total the person can run in the first hours; terrain slows running by the same ratio as walking. Nobody runs over 70 by default; --can-run yes/no overrides.

activity._source: ASSUMPTION. Share of each daylight / night hour spent actually moving, and a cap on moving hours per 24 h. 'likely' = a typical lost person who rests, hesitates and mostly stops at night; 'max' = keeps going as long as the body allows. Night speed multiplies speed after civil dusk (sun below -6 deg).

dementia._note: ASSUMPTION: people with dementia tend to keep walking and rest less, including at night.

night_by_age._note: ASSUMPTION, to calibrate: share of each dark hour spent moving, by age, per scenario (replaces likely/max night shares).

day_decay._note: ASSUMPTION, to calibrate: multiplier on the daily moving-hour cap for day 1, 2, 3, 4+ (fatigue, hunger, thirst, cold).

likely_cap._source: CALIBRATED 2026-10-13 on 70 solved cases (data/cases/; roads on; direction-unknown cases use the median walking time over all directions at the reported distance). The likely budget is min(cap, physical max); cap = 75th percentile of walking hours to the found point per group, because walking time does not grow with time missing. Leave-one-out coverage 71%; geographic hold-out 51% (international -> Türkiye) and 93% (Türkiye -> international). Re-fit with scripts/calibrate.py fit <dir> --write.

priority._source: Where people are found, by category. Directions come from published lost-person findings: hikers 42 % found on a trail, road or stream (Doke 2012, Yosemite); dementia: 66 % cross or leave a road, those not on a road are mostly within 15 m of one, 20 % found in structures, downhill 42 % vs uphill 19 % (Koester 2008 dementia chapter; Koester ICAR 2025); young children shelter in small spaces and sleep (NEWSAR training notes, UVA Today interview). The multipliers themselves are ASSUMPTIONS sized to those shares; calibrate when found points with coordinates are available.
priority._beyond_likely: ASSUMPTION: weight of a cell beyond the likely limit, falling linearly to 0 at the physical limit.

sweep_width_m._source: ASSUMPTION within published ranges: effective sweep width (m) of one searcher for a responsive-sized adult target, by ESA WorldCover class. Koopman's random-search law POD = 1 - exp(-W L / A) is the standard model in land SAR (Koester, Cooper, Frost, Robe 2004, 'Sweep width estimation for ground search and rescue', US Coast Guard / NASAR; Koopman 1946). Field-measured widths range from ~10 m in dense brush to over 60 m in open terrain. Calibrate with local sweep-width experiments when available; for small children or unresponsive people use lower values.

access._source: ASSUMPTION unless stated; used by access.py. Speeds are typical urban/rural driving speeds for emergency vehicles in normal conditions. Debris distances: a collapsed reinforced-concrete building spreads debris roughly up to a fraction of its height; Turkish urban residential blocks are mostly 4-8 storeys (12-25 m). A destroyed building is taken to close a narrow local street within 20 m and a wider road within 10 m (one lane may stay usable); a damaged building only slows traffic next to it. Calibrate against post-event road-status reports (e.g. AFAD / KGM road closure lists) when available.
access._carry_m: ASSUMPTION: a building counts as reachable when a vehicle can get within this distance (teams carry equipment and stretchers the rest).
